feedback: If a learner says the Sun moved, point to the lamp: it has not changed position — only the globe turned. The Sun's apparent movement comes from our spin.
If a learner thinks the whole Earth is dark at night, rotate the globe to show the opposite side is lit — it is day there right now.
If a learner says the Sun went out or was covered, point out the lamp is still shining on the far side; night is just our side turned away.
activities.intendedInsight: Day and night happen because Earth spins and our side turns to face or away from a Sun that stays put; it is always daytime somewhere on the other side.
learnerActions: In a darkened room, set up a single fixed light source (a lamp) as the Sun; it must not move.
Hold or stand a globe beside the lamp and stick a marker on your home town.
Slowly spin the globe and watch your marked town travel from the lit side (day) into the shadow side (night) and back again — one full turn = one day.
Describe out loud what is moving: say whether the Sun or the globe is turning.
Find and point to the terminator — the sharp line where day meets night on the globe.
activities.title: Spin into night: the globe and the fixed lamp

feedback: If a learner says one spin takes a year, slow down and separate the motions: a single turn is a day; the long walk around the Sun is the year.
If a learner attributes day/night to the orbit, return to the spin-only step — show day/night happening from turning in place, before any walking around.
Praise when a learner correctly labels each motion with its own effect and its own timescale.
activities.intendedInsight: Rotation (spin) and revolution (orbit) are two different motions on two very different timescales: one spin makes a day, one orbit makes a year. The orbit does NOT cause day and night.
learnerActions: First, practise only the spin: turn the globe one full rotation and name it 'one day, about 24 hours'.
Next, draw an orbit path on the floor with the Sun (lamp) at the centre.

Keep the globe spinning while you walk it all the way around the Sun; one full lap = one year, about 365 days. Remember that the real Earth spins about 365 times during one lap, far more than you can turn the globe while walking.
Say aloud which motion gives day/night (the spin) and which gives the year (the orbit).
Connect 365 days to the calendar year you already know.
activities.title: Two journeys, two clocks: separate spin from orbit

feedback: If a learner thinks the whole planet is dark at night, have them view the opposite hemisphere and see it in daylight.
Confirm understanding when a learner can locate both a day region and a night region at the same moment.
activities.intendedInsight: The Earth-Sun system is spatial: viewing the lit hemisphere from any angle makes it clear that day and night exist simultaneously on opposite sides of a spinning Earth.
learnerActions: Using a 3D model or by moving around a spinning globe, view the lit hemisphere from different angles.
Fly or walk to the terminator and look along the day/night boundary.
Travel to the far (night) side and confirm it is dark while the near side is in day.
Explain why it is always day somewhere on Earth at the same time.
activities.title: Explore the lit hemisphere from any angle

feedback: If a learner matches orbit to day/night, revisit the spin-only demonstration before re-sorting.
If a learner picks 'the Sun travels around Earth', return to the fixed-lamp model where the Sun never moves.
Encourage learners to say WHY, not just which answer, so you can hear which model they hold.
activities.intendedInsight: After building the motion intuition, learners can recall and apply the two facts and reject the common misconceptions.
learnerActions: Match each motion to its effect and its timescale: spin → day/night → ~24 hours; orbit → year → ~365 days.
Put the parts of a day in order as a spot rotates through dawn, noon, dusk, and midnight.
Answer a question that confronts the 'Sun moves' idea by choosing and justifying what really happens.
Explain in your own words why the orbit does not cause day and night.
activities.title: Check and sort: motion, effect, timescale
